section.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Gastric Cancer Surgery in China: Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center and Fudan Shanghai Compared
section.intro: These FAQs explain how gastric cancer surgery is performed at leading Chinese cancer centers and how Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center and Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center compare for international patients.

groups.title: Understanding Gastric Cancer Surgery in China

items.q: What is gastric cancer surgery and when is it needed?
items.a: Gastric cancer surgery removes part or all of the stomach along with nearby lymph nodes to treat stomach cancer. It is usually considered when the tumor is localized or locally advanced and the patient is fit for an operation. The exact procedure depends on tumor location, stage, and overall health. Surgery is often combined with chemotherapy, and the final plan should be decided by a qualified oncology and surgical team after full staging.

items.q: Why do international patients consider gastric cancer surgery in China?
items.a: Many international patients consider China because major centers perform very high volumes of gastric cancer surgery, which is linked to surgical experience. Gastric cancer is common in China, so leading hospitals have specialized upper-gastrointestinal teams, minimally invasive expertise, and structured multidisciplinary care. Costs may also be lower than in some Western countries. Suitability still depends on diagnosis, stage, and specialist review, and outcomes are never guaranteed for any individual patient.

items.q: What is Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center known for in gastric cancer?
items.a: Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center (SYSUCC) in Guangzhou is one of China's largest comprehensive cancer hospitals with a dedicated gastric surgery department. It is known for high surgical volumes, minimally invasive and radical gastrectomy, integrated chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and active clinical research. It treats many complex and advanced cases. Whether it suits a specific patient depends on cancer type, stage, and medical review by the treating oncology team.

items.q: What is Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center known for in gastric cancer?
items.a: Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center (FUSCC) is a leading Shanghai-based cancer hospital with a specialized gastric surgery team and strong multidisciplinary tumor boards. It is recognized for radical and minimally invasive gastrectomy, perioperative chemotherapy, pathology and biomarker testing, and clinical trials. It handles a large number of stomach cancer cases each year. Its suitability for an individual patient depends on stage, biomarker profile, and assessment by the treating specialists.

items.q: Who is eligible for gastric cancer surgery at these centers?
items.a: Eligibility for gastric cancer surgery generally depends on tumor stage, location, spread, and whether the patient is fit for anesthesia and recovery. Patients with localized or locally advanced disease are more likely to be considered, while widespread metastatic cancer may be treated differently. Both SYSUCC and FUSCC assess eligibility through imaging, endoscopy, and pathology. Final decisions are made by the surgical and oncology team after reviewing the complete medical record.

items.q: How should I choose between Sun Yat-sen and Fudan Shanghai?
items.a: Choosing between SYSUCC and FUSCC usually depends on location, case complexity, waiting time, and the specific surgical team's experience with your tumor type. Both are high-volume national cancer centers with strong gastric surgery programs, so the difference is often practical rather than one being clearly superior. It is wise to obtain a medical review and estimated plan from each. The most appropriate center should be confirmed with your treating oncology team.

items.q: What does the surgical process involve step by step?
items.a: The gastric cancer surgery process typically begins with staging tests such as endoscopy, biopsy, and CT scans, followed by a multidisciplinary treatment plan. Some patients receive chemotherapy before surgery. The operation may be a partial or total gastrectomy with lymph node removal, done openly or via minimally invasive techniques. Recovery includes monitoring, nutrition support, and follow-up. The exact steps depend on stage and are guided by the treating team.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of gastric cancer surgery?
items.a: Like all major surgery, gastric cancer surgery carries risks including bleeding, infection, anastomotic leak, and anesthesia-related complications. Longer-term effects can include weight loss, difficulty eating, dumping syndrome, and vitamin deficiencies, especially after total stomach removal. These risks vary with the patient's health, stage, and extent of surgery. Experienced high-volume teams aim to reduce complications, but no procedure is risk-free, and risks should be discussed directly with the surgical team.

items.q: How much does gastric cancer surgery cost in China?
items.a: The cost of gastric cancer surgery in China varies widely and cannot be quoted as a fixed price. Estimates typically depend on the hospital, type of gastrectomy, length of stay, tests, chemotherapy, and any complications. International patient pricing may differ from local rates. Some patients find costs lower than in Western countries, but this is not guaranteed. A personalized estimate should be requested from the hospital after medical record review.

items.q: Is gastric cancer surgery in China available to international patients?
items.a: Yes, both SYSUCC and FUSCC treat international patients, but access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, visa approval, and fitness to travel. International patients usually need translated medical reports, imaging, and pathology before an opinion can be given. Waiting times, language support, and admission processes vary. Nothing about admission, cost, or outcome is guaranteed, and each hospital decides suitability after reviewing the patient's diagnosis and overall condition.

items.q: Which other countries offer high-quality gastric cancer surgery?
items.a: High-quality gastric cancer surgery is also available in countries such as Japan, South Korea, India, Singapore, Germany, and the United States, many of which are recognized for upper-gastrointestinal expertise. The best choice depends on cost, travel distance, waiting time, and the patient's stage and needs. Comparing centers by surgical volume and multidisciplinary care is helpful. The final decision should always be guided by a qualified oncology team after reviewing the case.

items.q: Do these centers offer minimally invasive or robotic gastrectomy?
items.a: Both Sun Yat-sen and Fudan Shanghai cancer centers offer minimally invasive gastrectomy, including laparoscopic surgery, and robotic approaches may be available in selected cases. These techniques can mean smaller incisions and faster recovery for suitable patients, but they are not appropriate for every tumor. Whether minimally invasive or open surgery is chosen depends on tumor size, location, and stage. The surgical team decides the safest approach for each patient.

items.q: Are clinical trials available for gastric cancer at these hospitals?
items.a: Both SYSUCC and FUSCC are active in gastric cancer research and may run clinical trials involving chemotherapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy, or new surgical approaches. Trials are not open to everyone, since each has strict inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligibility is decided only after medical record review and investigator assessment. Enrollment and benefit can never be guaranteed, and trial participation should be discussed carefully with the treating oncology and research team.

items.q: Is chemotherapy or immunotherapy combined with surgery?
items.a: Gastric cancer surgery is often combined with additional treatments such as chemotherapy before or after the operation, and immunotherapy or targeted therapy may be considered for selected patients based on biomarker testing. This multimodal approach aims to reduce recurrence risk in appropriate cases. The exact combination depends on stage, tumor biology, and biomarkers like HER2 or PD-L1. The full plan should be determined by a multidisciplinary oncology team.

items.q: What medical reports are needed before treatment in China?
items.a: Before a Chinese cancer center can review a case, international patients usually need recent endoscopy and biopsy results, pathology reports, CT or PET-CT imaging, blood tests, and a summary of previous treatments. Reports may need translation into Chinese or English. Complete and up-to-date records help the team give an accurate opinion and estimate. Missing information can delay assessment, so gathering documents early is helpful before requesting any hospital review.

items.q: How do international patients plan travel and follow-up care?
items.a: Planning travel for gastric cancer surgery involves arranging a medical visa, confirming hospital admission, and allowing time for recovery before returning home. Access depends on visa approval, hospital acceptance, and fitness to travel, none of which are guaranteed. Follow-up care, including scans, nutrition support, and further chemotherapy, may be shared between the Chinese center and doctors at home. A clear follow-up plan should be discussed with the treating team before travel.

items.q: Should I get a second opinion before choosing surgery abroad?
items.a: Yes, obtaining a second opinion is strongly encouraged before choosing gastric cancer surgery abroad. A second review can confirm the diagnosis, stage, and whether surgery is the right option, and may compare recommendations from different centers. This helps patients make informed decisions and avoid unnecessary travel. Second opinions do not guarantee a particular treatment or outcome, and final decisions should always rest with a qualified oncology team reviewing the full record.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with gastric cancer surgery in China?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organize medical reports, identify relevant specialists or treatment centers, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. For gastric cancer surgery, this can include sharing records with centers such as Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center and Fudan University Shanghai Cancer Center for review. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, and overall health.
